lessons.title: Food chains, energy flow, the carbon cycle and conservation
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Biology — Ecology: food chains and webs, pyramids, energy flow, carbon cycle, conservation (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original text written for the GCE O Level Biology syllabus; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Construct and interpret food chains, food webs and ecological pyramids.
Explain why energy is lost along a food chain and calculate the efficiency of energy transfer.
Describe the carbon cycle and give reasons and methods for conservation.

blocks.title: Key words
blocks.md:
- **Habitat**: the place where an organism lives.
- **Population**: all the organisms of one species in an area.
- **Community**: all the populations of different species in an area.
- **Ecosystem**: a community together with its physical environment (soil, water, air).
- **Trophic level**: the feeding position of an organism in a food chain.

blocks.title: Producers, consumers, decomposers
blocks.md:
- **Producers** (green plants) make their own food by photosynthesis.
- **Primary consumers** (herbivores) eat producers.
- **Secondary consumers** eat primary consumers; **tertiary consumers** eat secondary consumers.
- **Decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste, returning nutrients to the soil.

blocks.title: Food chains and food webs
blocks.md:
A **food chain** shows how energy passes from one organism to the next. The **arrow** points in the direction of **energy flow**: from the food to the eater.

A **food web** is a set of interconnected food chains. It is more realistic, because most animals eat more than one kind of food.

blocks.caption: A savanna food chain: the arrows show the direction of energy flow.
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a row joined by arrows pointing right: grass, grasshopper, lizard, hawk. Under them: producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer.

blocks.title: Energy flow
blocks.md:
- The **Sun** is the source of energy for almost all ecosystems. Producers capture only a small part of it.
- At each trophic level, only about **10 %** of the energy is passed on to the next level.
- The rest is lost: as **heat** from respiration, in movement, in faeces and urine, and in parts that are not eaten (bones, roots).
- This is why food chains rarely have more than **four or five** links.

blocks.title: Efficiency of energy transfer
blocks.md: Both energies must be in the same unit (usually kJ). The answer is a percentage.
blocks.tex: \text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{energy passed to the next level}}{\text{energy in the previous level}} \times 100

blocks.title: Ecological pyramids
blocks.md:
- A **pyramid of numbers** shows the number of organisms at each level. It can be **inverted**: one mango tree can feed hundreds of caterpillars.
- A **pyramid of biomass** shows the dry mass at each level.
- A **pyramid of energy** shows the energy at each level. It is **always** a true pyramid, because energy is lost at every level.

blocks.title: Method: food web and pyramid questions
blocks.md:
1. Find the producer: no arrow points to it.
2. Follow the arrows from food to eater to write a chain.
3. Give each organism its trophic level in **that** chain (it may differ in another chain).
4. For energy: apply the efficiency formula, or take about 10 % per level.
5. To predict the effect of a change, follow **every** arrow into and out of the organism concerned.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: a pyramid of energy
blocks.statement: The pyramid shows the energy (kJ per m² per year) at each level of a food chain in a grassland. Calculate the efficiency of transfer from producers to herbivores, and explain why the pyramid gets narrower.

steps.md: Energy in the producers: 20 000 kJ. Energy passed to the herbivores: 2 000 kJ.
The other 90 % is lost: heat from respiration, movement, faeces, and plant parts not eaten.
Because energy is lost at every level, less energy is available to each level above: the bars get narrower.

blocks.answer: **Efficiency = 10 %. The pyramid narrows because most energy is lost (mainly as heat) at each level.**

blocks.title: Worked example 2: predicting a change in a food web
blocks.statement: In a food web, grass is eaten by grasshoppers and rats; lizards eat grasshoppers; snakes eat lizards and rats. Hunters kill most of the snakes. Predict what happens to the rats and the grass.

steps.md: Find what eats rats: only snakes in this web. With fewer snakes, fewer rats are eaten.
So the **rat population increases** (at least for a while).
More rats eat more grass: the amount of **grass decreases**.
Lizards, also eaten by snakes, may increase too, and then eat more grasshoppers: a change spreads through the whole web.

blocks.answer: **Rats increase because they have fewer predators; the grass then decreases because it is eaten by more rats.**

blocks.title: The carbon cycle
blocks.md:
- **Photosynthesis** removes carbon dioxide from the air and turns it into carbohydrates.
- Carbon passes to animals by **feeding**.
- **Respiration** by plants, animals and decomposers returns CO2 to the air.
- Remains that do not decay can form **fossil fuels** (coal, oil, gas) over millions of years.
- **Combustion** of fuels and wood releases CO2.

blocks.caption: The carbon cycle: processes that remove carbon dioxide from the air and processes that return it.
blocks.alt: Boxes for carbon dioxide in the air, green plants, animals, decomposers and fossil fuels, joined by arrows labelled photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, death and decay, and combustion.

blocks.title: Conservation
blocks.md:
**Why conserve?** To protect biodiversity, food and medicine sources, soils and water, and to limit climate change (forests store carbon).

**How?**
- National parks and reserves, such as Korup National Park, Waza National Park and the Dja Faunal Reserve in Cameroon.
- Laws against poaching and the hunting of protected species.
- Reforestation and agroforestry; controlled logging.
- Fishing quotas and minimum net mesh sizes.
- Education, recycling and reducing pollution.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Drawing arrows from the eater to the food: the arrow points **to the eater**.
- Saying energy is "used up" or "destroyed": it is **transferred**, mostly as heat.
- Saying energy is recycled like carbon: **carbon cycles**, energy **flows** one way.
- Forgetting that decomposers **respire** and release CO2.
- Thinking a pyramid of numbers is always pyramid-shaped.

items: The Dja Faunal Reserve in southern Cameroon is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, home to gorillas, chimpanzees and forest elephants.
Burning forests to clear land releases carbon dioxide and, at the same time, removes the trees that would have absorbed it by photosynthesis.

reviewNotes: Check the list of Cameroonian protected areas and their current status (Korup, Waza, Dja) before publication.
The '10 % rule' is an approximation; check that the syllabus uses this figure.

exercises.prompt: In a food chain, what does each arrow show?
choices: The direction in which energy flows
The direction in which the animals move
Which organism eats the other, pointing from eater to food
exercises.explanation: The arrow goes from the food to the organism that eats it: it shows the flow of energy.
mistakes: Drawing arrows from the eater to the food.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: In the food chain: cassava leaves → grasshopper → lizard → hawk, the lizard is...
exercises.explanation: The lizard eats the grasshopper, which is a primary consumer (herbivore): the lizard is a secondary consumer.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: True or false: decomposers return carbon dioxide to the air through their respiration.
exercises.explanation: True. Bacteria and fungi respire as they digest dead matter, releasing carbon dioxide.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: The primary consumers of a pond receive 15 000 kJ of energy per year. The secondary consumers receive 1 200 kJ per year. Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer between these two levels.
exercises.method: Efficiency = energy passed on ÷ energy in the previous level × 100.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Match each process of the carbon cycle with its description.
pairs: Removes carbon dioxide from the air
Releases carbon dioxide from glucose in living cells
Releases carbon dioxide by burning fuels
Releases carbon dioxide from dead organisms
Locks carbon in coal, oil and gas for millions of years
exercises.explanation: Only photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air. Respiration, combustion and decomposition return it. Fossilisation stores carbon for a very long time.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: The diagram shows part of a food web in a grassland of the Adamawa plateau.
exercises.method: Follow the arrows from food to eater; for predictions, look at every arrow into and out of the organism.
mistakes: Reversing the arrows when writing a food chain.
Predicting only one effect when asked to explain.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.explanation: No arrow points to the grass: it makes its own food by photosynthesis.

parts.prompt: Which food chain can be taken from this web?
parts.explanation: Each arrow of this chain exists in the web. Rats do not eat lizards here, and the other chains have arrows in the wrong direction.

parts.prompt: The grass holds 40 000 kJ per m² per year, and the grasshoppers obtain 3 200 kJ of it. Calculate the percentage efficiency of this transfer.
A disease kills most of the snakes. Suggest and explain the effect on the rat population.
parts.model: The rat population increases (1 mark) because fewer rats are eaten by snakes (fewer predators) (1 mark). Accept: hawks may eat more rats, which limits the increase.
rubric: 1 mark: explanation: fewer predators / fewer rats eaten.
parts.explanation: Removing a predator usually lets its prey increase, until food becomes limiting or other predators eat more of it.

parts.prompt: Why does this web have no animal that eats hawks?
choices: Too little energy reaches the top of the food chain to support another level
Hawks are too fast to be caught
parts.explanation: Energy is lost at each level, so very little is left at the top: not enough to support a further trophic level.

exercises.prompt: What is the original source of energy for almost every food chain?
exercises.explanation: Producers capture light energy from the Sun by photosynthesis; this energy then passes along the chain.

exercises.prompt: Approximately what fraction of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next?
exercises.explanation: Only about 10 % is transferred; about 90 % is lost, mostly as heat.

exercises.prompt: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
exercises.explanation: Photosynthesis takes in CO2; the other three processes release it.

exercises.prompt: Which type of pyramid is always pyramid-shaped (never inverted)?
exercises.explanation: Energy decreases at every level, so the pyramid of energy always narrows upwards. A pyramid of numbers can be inverted.

choices: Using fishing nets with a very small mesh
exercises.explanation: A national park protects habitats and species. The other three reduce biodiversity.

exercises.prompt: Question 4 — Ecology (5 marks). In a forest ecosystem, trees are eaten by caterpillars, caterpillars by birds, and birds by eagles.
exercises.method: Give precise reasons in explanations; use the 10 % rule only when the question says so.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

parts.prompt: Which statement about the eagles is correct?
The caterpillars obtain 50 000 kJ of energy. Assuming that 10 % is passed on at each level, how much energy (in kJ) reaches the birds?
Large areas of this forest are cut down and burnt. What is the effect on the carbon dioxide concentration of the air?
choices: It increases: burning releases CO2 and fewer trees remove it by photosynthesis
It decreases: burning removes CO2 from the air
It does not change, because the carbon cycle is balanced
parts.explanation: Combustion releases the carbon stored in the wood, and the loss of trees reduces the removal of CO2 by photosynthesis.

parts.prompt: State two measures that can be taken to conserve forests and their wildlife in Cameroon.
parts.model: Any two: create or protect national parks and reserves; enforce laws against poaching; reforestation / agroforestry; controlled (sustainable) logging; education of local communities.
rubric: 1 mark for each valid measure, maximum 2.
Vague answers such as "protect nature" score 0.
parts.explanation: Conservation combines protecting habitats, controlling exploitation and restoring damaged areas.
